purpose: Ivosidenib is used to treat certain types of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and a type of bile duct cancer called cholangiocarcinoma. It is specifically used in patients whose cancer has a certain gene mutation called an IDH1 mutation. Your doctor will test for this mutation before prescribing this medicine.
how_it_works: In some cancers, a faulty gene called IDH1 causes cancer cells to grow out of control. Ivosidenib works by blocking this faulty IDH1 protein, which helps slow down or stop cancer cells from growing. Think of it like a key that fits into and blocks a broken switch inside the cancer cell, helping to turn off what was driving the cancer.
common_side_effects: Some common side effects include feeling tired or weak, nausea, diarrhea, belly pain, decreased appetite, joint or muscle aches, swelling in your legs or arms, shortness of breath, cough, and changes in your blood counts. Some patients may also notice changes in their heart rhythm, so your doctor will monitor your heart with regular EKGs.
warnings: This medication can sometimes cause a serious condition called differentiation syndrome, which can cause fever, trouble breathing, swelling, low blood pressure, and fluid buildup — contact your doctor right away if you notice these symptoms. It can also cause changes in heart rhythm (QT prolongation), so tell your doctor about all other medications you take. This drug can harm an unborn baby, so women who could become pregnant and men with partners who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for a period after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 500 mg taken by mouth once a day. It can be taken with or without food. Try to take it at the same time each day. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush or split it. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day, but skip it if it is almost time for your next dose.
